newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: OPINION-From the Beehive-Nats take business flak.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-From the Beehive-Nats take business flak.

text.p: WELLINGTON, April 4 - Prime Minister Jim Bolger must be starting to feel a bit tetchy about the reaction from lobby groups to the government's spending plans.

He told a government to business forum in Wellington this week that he hoped business leaders complaining about the extra spending would be just as noisy come Budget night when the health and education lobbyists were crying "insufficient".

Of course writing Budgets has always been an exercise in giving less than some want and more than others want to give through taxes. But with monetary conditions continuing to put the heat on exporters there are added pressure to restrict spending.

Add to that the inevitable compromises which coalition building brought and the government is left -- perhaps for the first time since 1984 -- putting up with scepticism about its strategy even from the dry end of the business community which has for so long been a cheerleader of the reform process.

Some, such as Labour Minister Max Bradford and ACC Minister Jenny Shipley are managing to steer the middle ground between further reform and alienating their NZ First coalition partner, mainly because the areas they operate in have never been "litmus" issues for NZ First.

The problem Bolger is facing with his business support base was highlighted at the finance and expenditure select committee meeting on Wednesday where The Business Roundtable, manufacturers and unionists joined in condemning the spending plans, albeit for differing reasons.

All agreed that the redistributive effects of the Budget Policy Statement, notably the abolition of targeting of pensions through the scraping of the surtax and the extra assistance for tertiary students, were unfair.
The Roundtable, through chief executive Roger Kerr, saw no logic in redistributing more social spending upwards. The Roundtable has consistently favoured tax cuts.

The unions, via Council of Trade Unions (CTU) economist Peter Harris, saw no real distinction between the tax cuts (which they said favoured the young) and extra spending (which they said favoured the old). Harris saw it as a family argument
within National between the comfortable old and the comfortable young.
All of the opinions trotted out before the committee were interesting but ultimately doomed to near irrelevance.
The committee's examination of the BPS is a sideshow.

It picks over the broad fiscal parameters (for details see June's Budget), while not 50 metres away in the Beehive ministers are finalising "bilaterals" between the Treasury Ministers and the various departments that put the final touches on the Budget.
The chances of the committee's deliberations and its report to parliament -- sometime in the next month -- having any effect on the Budget are somewhere between nil and zero.
All of which is starting to get palpably under the skin of committee members and those making submissions.
Chair Tony Ryall has already signalled the need for a review of the timing of the BPS in an interview with Reuters. He would move it to January.
The CTU thinks the fourth quarter would be more useful -- around the time of the December Economic and Fiscal Update when the fiscal parameters are clear.
The optimists said, without any real conviction, that at least the process is transparent and perhaps, just perhaps, submissions made this year will have some impact next year.
United MP Peter Dunne pointed out that if the BPS itself is a political statement then so are the submissions.
Harris agreed with a shrug but pointed out silence would be construed as assent. Catch 22.

When former Finance Minister Ruth Richardson promoted the Fiscal Responsibility Act and the financial reporting regime which includes the BPS, it was to ensure transparency and to put a brake on MMP which she feared would quickly undermine the
economic reforms.
What she didn't envisage was that one of the bulwarks of her reforms would itself become the object of disgruntlement because of its impotence.

It now seems certain that the report from the committee will reveal a cross-party will to make the examination of the Budget process more relevant. That may not answer all of business leaders' concerns but it may give them a more relevant forum to air them.
(Note - The opinions expressed in this article represent the views of the author only. They should not be seen as reflecting the views of Reuters.)
